chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
The certificate of location is one of the most important — and most misunderstood — documents in a Quebec real-estate transaction. An outdated or non-compliant certificate can delay, complicate, or derail a sale.

This guide explains what this document is, when it must be renewed, what irregularities it can reveal, and how to plan ahead for it as a seller.

Informational content: special cases are settled with the notary and the land surveyor. Each chapter ends with a lined « My notes » page.

chapters.title: What is a certificate of location?
chapters.objective: Understand the role of this surveying document.
chapters.html:
Understand the role of this surveying document.

The certificate of location is a document prepared by a land surveyor that describes the current state of the property: lot boundaries, location of the buildings, easements, any encroachments, and compliance with regulations and titles.

It includes a plan and a report. It allows the buyer, the lender, and the notary to know exactly what is being sold and whether everything is compliant.

Emilie's tip

Think of the certificate of location as the property's « ID card ». It is what confirms that what you are selling truly matches the titles and the regulations.

chapters.title: When is a new certificate required?
chapters.objective: Know whether yours is still valid.
chapters.html:
Know whether yours is still valid.

A certificate can become inadequate if it is too old or if it no longer reflects the current state of the premises. The notary and the lender require a certificate that matches present reality.

  • Too old: standards and the state of the premises may have changed.
  • Changes since (addition, shed, pool, fence, driveway): the certificate does not show them.
  • A regulatory or boundary change: can make it non-compliant.

When in doubt, order a new certificate from a land surveyor. It takes time: it is best to start early.

Emilie's tip

If you have added anything since your certificate (shed, pool, addition), assume it needs updating. Plan ahead: a surveyor does not produce a certificate overnight.

chapters.title: The irregularities it can reveal
chapters.objective: Anticipate the problems to resolve before the sale.
chapters.html:
Anticipate the problems to resolve before the sale.

  • Encroachment: a building (yours or a neighbour's) that crosses the boundary.
  • Easement: a third party's right over your land (right of way, public utility).
  • Non-compliance with setbacks or municipal by-laws.
  • A discrepancy between reality and the titles.

Some irregularities are minor; others require corrective work, regularization, or negotiation. Discovering them early prevents them from blocking the sale at the last minute.

Emilie's tip

Have the notary review your certificate BEFORE listing. Resolving an irregularity up front is far simpler than discovering it under pressure with an offer in hand.

chapters.title: Costs, timelines, and planning ahead
chapters.html:
Plan for this often-overlooked item.

A new certificate involves a cost (the surveyor's fees, which vary by property) and, above all, a production timeline. In a sale, that timeline can be critical if you leave it too late.

  • Check your certificate as soon as you consider selling.
  • Order a new one early if needed.
  • Build this cost and timeline into your sale schedule.
Emilie's tip

Treat the certificate of location as the very first box to check off in your sale. It is the document that, when forgotten, most often delays a signing at the notary's office.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, in concrete terms.

This week

  1. Find my certificate of location and check its date.
  2. List the additions made since (shed, pool, extension).

Within 30 days

  1. Have the notary review the certificate.
  2. Order a new certificate if needed, early.

Then

  1. Resolve any irregularity before listing.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Certificate of location: a surveying document describing the state of the property.
  • Land surveyor: the professional who produces the certificate.
  • Encroachment: a building that crosses a lot boundary.
  • Easement: a third party's right over your property.
  • Non-compliance: a discrepancy with the regulations or the titles.
